summary: More than 150 Chinese apps, WeChat and Alipay among them, have shut ByteDance's AI phone assistant out. Beijing also issued a plan to put more AI into consumer goods.
body: China's biggest apps are refusing to let an AI assistant use them on a user's behalf. ByteDance's Doubao assistant can tap and type its way through other apps, a method called GUI automation (the AI works the on-screen buttons the way a person would). It runs on Nubia's NaviX Ultra phone, which went on sale Sept. 16 [^1][^2]. On Oct. 14, Doubao posted a list of more than 150 apps that have opted out. Nearly 60% belong to Tencent or Alibaba, including WeChat and Alipay. Meituan, Didi, Xiaohongshu, several banks and the rival AI apps DeepSeek and Kimi are also on it [^1]. People can still use these apps by hand. The assistant just cannot do tasks inside them for you [^1][^2]. A Tsinghua University researcher told Chinese media that China has no rules yet on how AI agents may operate other companies' apps [^1].

Beijing is pushing in the same direction from the policy side. On Oct. 19, the Ministry of Commerce and eight other government departments issued guidelines on what they call technology-driven commerce. The guidelines call for more AI in manufacturing and more smart products such as phones, PCs and robots [^3]. Chinese state media says the plan is meant to lift spending on both goods and services [^4]. My read: the government wants AI in everyday devices, but the Doubao dispute shows the big platforms still decide how far an assistant can reach.

Outside China, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has ordered civilian federal agencies to remove products from the Chinese AI company DeepSeek and to stop buying them, according to reporting that cites Bloomberg and Reuters. The order points to data security concerns [^5]. On the everyday side, Duolingo launched a course of about 50 lessons in Shanghainese, a local dialect that about 10 million people speak. Shanghainese has faded as schools promote Mandarin, and this is the app's second Chinese dialect after Cantonese [^6].
differences: The reason for the opt-outs is disputed. None of the listed app makers had publicly commented as of Monday [^1]. Caixin describes the dispute as a clash over data compliance, privacy and automated access [^2]. A Tsinghua researcher quoted by Sixth Tone said privacy concerns make the refusals understandable, but that they may also protect the platforms' own AI ecosystems from a rival [^1].

reads.title: China's Agentic AI Controversy
reads.summary: Background from March 2026. Samm Sacks, of New America and Yale Law School, explains why the Doubao phone set off a fight over data, privacy and platform power, and what other countries might learn from it.
